blocks.text: The Output Isn't What You Pictured — Now What?

You ran the prompt, and the result came back fine, but you still feel like it's not right. The colors are off, the mood is wrong, or it just looks like something you've seen a hundred times. Starting over feels wasteful. There's a faster way.
Every Weak Output Has a Cause

When an AI design tool produces something generic, it's not random. One of the four prompt components that you've covered in the previous lesson — visual type, audience, style, or mood — was either missing or too vague. The tool filled the gap with its own defaults.
Don't fix it with "try again" and the same prompt. Instead, find the weak part and replace it with something specific.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! "Adventurous" covers mood. "Banner" covers visual type. But no audience means no tonal reference, and no style means the tool picks something safe and generic.

feedbackIncorrect.text: "Banner" does give the visual type, and dimensions aren't part of the four-part structure. The missing pieces are audience and style — without them, AI opts for default.

blocks.question: This prompt returned a flat, forgettable result: "Create a social media banner for Roamly. The design should feel adventurous." Which components are missing?

blocks.text: Choosing the Right Tool

You've identified what's missing from the prompt, but what's also important to consider is where you run it. For social media banners, Canva's Magic Media is the strongest fit. It generates images directly inside the editor, so you can adjust sizing, swap brand colors, and layer text without switching apps.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Perfect! I've created four social media banner options for Roamly that capture that cinematic, adventurous spirit.
The designs showcase untamed landscapes and open paths that speak to the off-the-beaten-path experiences your audience craves. Feel free to customize any of these with your specific messaging, logo, or brand colors!
blocks.prompt: Roamly is a travel app for independent adventurers. Add the two missing components to sharpen the banner prompt.
blocks.template: Create a social media banner for Roamly. The target audience is [audience] seeking [travel style]. Style: [style direction]. The design should feel adventurous and free.

blocks.text: This is what Canva AI returned. All the variations match the description, but give you options to choose what you like more.

Two targeted additions do make a difference. The audience told the tool who it's speaking to. The style told it how the visual should look. The mood was already there — it just finally had something to work with.
Prompt refinement means editing, not rewriting. Find the component that failed, replace it with something specific, and regenerate. Everything else stays exactly as it was.
blocks.title: 💡 One Variable at a Time

blocks.text: Constraints Lock the Style

Fixing a missing component gets you closer. But let's say you specifically don't want your visuals to have faces, text overlays, or other noise. Constraints close that gap. They don't add to the output; they cut from it. "No text overlays, no faces, wide landscape only" removes an entire category of defaults.

blocks.text: Compare the results. The last variations came back far more minimalistic. The "Avoid" command didn't restrict creativity but redirected it toward what the brief needed.
Constraints in Midjourney

In Canva, you can type the constraints in the prompt as a simple instruction. Midjourney does the same thing differently — it uses a --no parameter at the end of the prompt. The syntax changes, but the logic stays the same.

blocks.prompt: Add the --no parameter in the prompt for FocusShift's logo.
blocks.template: FocusShift logo, minimalist icon, red and orange colors, flat vector style [negative prompt parameter] [elements to exclude]

blocks.text: The --no parameter works like a filter — it narrows what Midjourney pulls from, so the output stays inside the visual range you defined.

Specificity tells the tool what you want, constraints tell it what you don't. Together, they compress the output range to something close to the brief. Use both. In Canva, constraints go in the text prompt. In Midjourney, add --no [elements] at the end of your prompt.
blocks.title: 💡 Constraints Cut Noise

blocks.text: The Same Logic Works for Words

Back to FocusShift. The landing page has a logo, and now it needs words: a headline, a tagline, and a call-to-action. ChatGPT handles this, and the prompt structure is the same one you've been using in Canva.
The four components stay the same, but with a slight shift.

• Visual type = content type
  • Style direction = tone
  • Audience and mood carry over unchanged

blocks.exampleResponse:
Headline: Your best work happens in 25 minutes
Tagline: A simple way to manage deep work with steady, timed sessions, so you can stay present, make progress, and finish what matters.
CTA: Start a focused session

The headline and tagline are specific because the tone ruled out corporate language. The CTA is direct because the mood ruled out anything pressuring.

A Brand Needs More Than a Logo

In the previous lessons, you've created a logo and landing page copy for FocusShift, a productivity app. That's a great start, but hand it to another designer tomorrow, and they'll ask: what's the visual style? Warm or clinical? Bold or soft? Dark or light?

Right now, you don't have an answer, and without one, every next design decision starts from zero. This lesson solves the challenge.
A Direction or Endless Decisions
A common first instinct is to treat a logo as enough visual direction and skip straight to building assets — social posts, landing pages, UI screens.
The result is a brand that looks slightly different everywhere it appears. This happens because no one agreed on what it was supposed to look like before execution started.

blocks.text: Start With Three Directions
The mistake most people make is committing to a visual style before they've seen the alternatives. Three directions side by side reveal which one fits.
For FocusShift, these directions are worth exploring:

• Direction A: Productivity as a system. It's clean and clinical: white space, structured grids, sharp sans-serif type.
  • Direction B: Productivity as a habit. It's warm and human: soft textures, rounded shapes, muted earth tones.
  • Direction C: Productivity as a focus. It's bold and minimal: high contrast, heavy typography, dark backgrounds.

All three are credible for a productivity app. But credible isn't the same as right. FocusShift's audience — adults aged 40-60 building focus habits — will respond to one of these and scroll past the other two. Let's use AI to generate options, and you decide which one fits.

Collect, Don't Just Generate

Once you've picked a direction, the next step is strengthening it. AI outputs get you to a starting point. Real-world references — Pinterest, competitor sites, editorial photography — show how that style performs on an actual screen, in print, or in a social feed.
Lock the Style in Midjourney

Once you have references worth keeping — AI outputs, screenshots, saved images — Midjourney's Moodboard is where they come together. You upload the images, Midjourney analyzes their color, composition, and patterns, and generates a unique code that encodes that aesthetic. Add that code to any future prompt, and the style carries over.
Step 1 — Create a Moodboard
Here's how to build one:

1. Open Midjourney and click Moodboard in the left-side navigation.
  2. Hit My First Moodboard or New Moodboard and give it a name.
Step 2 — Add References
Add your references: drag and drop images, paste image URLs, or pull directly from your Midjourney gallery. Once the board is populated, Midjourney generates a unique ID for it.
Step 3 — Lock the Style
Copy that ID and add it to any prompt using --p mID — the moodboard style applies automatically. From that point on, every prompt you run with that code is anchored to the same visual language.

blocks.text: A Brand Needs More Than a Logo

In the previous lessons, you've created a logo and landing page copy for FocusShift, a productivity app. That's a great start, but hand it to another designer tomorrow, and they'll ask: what's the visual style? Warm or clinical? Bold or soft? Dark or light?

Right now, you don't have an answer, and without one, every next design decision starts from zero. This lesson solves the challenge.
A Direction or Endless Decisions
A common first instinct is to treat a logo as enough visual direction and skip straight to building assets — social posts, landing pages, UI screens.
The result is a brand that looks slightly different everywhere it appears. This happens because no one agreed on what it was supposed to look like before execution started.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Designers don't default to consistency. They go with what feels right in the moment, and, without a reference, "right" shifts from post to post. That's the problem a moodboard solves.

blocks.text: Start With Three Directions
The mistake most people make is committing to a visual style before they've seen the alternatives. Three directions side by side reveal which one fits.
For FocusShift, these directions are worth exploring:

• Direction A: Productivity as a system. It's clean and clinical: white space, structured grids, sharp sans-serif type.
  • Direction B: Productivity as a habit. It's warm and human: soft textures, rounded shapes, muted earth tones.
  • Direction C: Productivity as a focus. It's bold and minimal: high contrast, heavy typography, dark backgrounds.

All three are credible for a productivity app. But credible isn't the same as right. FocusShift's audience — adults aged 40-60 building focus habits — will respond to one of these and scroll past the other two. Let's use AI to generate options, and you decide which one fits.

blocks.text: Three Directions
You now have three generated visual directions. Run each through the two filters:

• Audience fit: Which direction speaks to adults aged 40-60 who are building focus habits?
  • Tone fit: Which direction matches the copy — "Your best work happens in 25 minutes"?
The direction that passes both filters is the one to lock.

The verdict is: Direction B fits FocusShift's tone — warm, supportive, not pressuring — and matches the copy. "Your best work happens in 25 minutes" is a calm promise that doesn't feel like a performance target.
Collect, Don't Just Generate

Once you've picked a direction, the next step is strengthening it. AI outputs get you to a starting point. Real-world references — Pinterest, competitor sites, editorial photography — show how that style performs on an actual screen, in print, or in a social feed.
Lock the Style in Midjourney

Once you have references worth keeping — AI outputs, screenshots, saved images — Midjourney's Moodboard is where they come together. You upload the images, Midjourney analyzes their color, composition, and patterns, and generates a unique code that encodes that aesthetic. Add that code to any future prompt, and the style carries over.
Step 1 — Create a Moodboard
Here's how to build one:

1. Open Midjourney and click Moodboard in the left-side navigation.
  2. Hit My First Moodboard or New Moodboard and give it a name.
Step 2 — Add References
Add your references: drag and drop images, paste image URLs, or pull directly from your Midjourney gallery. Once the board is populated, Midjourney generates a unique ID for it.
Step 3 — Lock the Style
Copy that ID and add it to any prompt using --p mID — the moodboard style applies automatically. From that point on, every prompt you run with that code is anchored to the same visual language.

blocks.text: A Direction in Your Head Isn't a Brand Kit

FocusShift has a locked visual direction — warm, human, sage, and terracotta, rounded type. You know what it looks like. But knowing isn't something you can hand to a tool, a collaborator, or your future self at 11 p.m. trying to finish a social post. A brand kit is.
What Is a Brand Kit?
A brand kit is a single document that records every visual decision: the exact colors with hex codes, the fonts and how to use them, and the style rules that keep everything consistent.
Start With Color

The moodboard established warm sage, sand, and terracotta as the FocusShift palette. But "warm sage" means something different to different AI tools. One will reach for a muted olive, another for a grey-green. A hex code removes this confusion. It locks the exact color so every tool, collaborator, and future design starts from the same point.
Colors also need roles: primary, secondary, and accent. Once each color has a job, it gets easy for you to create consistent designs.

blocks.text: Typography Carries Tone

FocusShift's direction is warm and human: rounded forms, soft textures, and approachable. The fonts need to carry the same feeling. A sharp geometric serif typeface would contradict everything the color palette is saying.
A brand kit uses two fonts:

• A headline font for titles and anything that needs presence
  • A body font for paragraphs, captions, and interface text
They need to work together without competing.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Lobster is decorative and playful — closer to a bakery sign than a productivity app. Times New Roman reads formal and dated. Neither carries the warm, supportive tone FocusShift needs.

blocks.question: FocusShift's direction is warm, rounded, and approachable — targeting adults aged 40-60. Which font pairing fits best?

blocks.text: Nunito and Lato aren't the only valid pairing, but the logic behind the choice is what matters. The headline font sets the tone, and the body font supports it. Both should feel like the same brand.

If you want to find your own pairing, Google Fonts is the most practical starting point: filter by category, preview combinations side by side, and check that both fonts are free to use. Search for the visual quality you're after — "rounded," "humanist," "geometric" — and compare how the headline and body read together at actual size.
blocks.title: Pro Tip

blocks.text: Put It Together in Canva

Canva's Brand Kit feature is where all of this gets documented in one place. Colors with hex codes, font pairings with size roles, and a logo — all stored so every design you open starts from the same foundation.
Setting it up takes less time than rebuilding it from scratch on your next project. Once it's there, Canva applies it to any template you open.
Write the Style Rules
The Canva Brand Kit stores the assets. The final step is turning them into a presentation — a document that explains the decisions behind them.
Canva has this built in: the Add guidelines feature lets you create a brand kit presentation directly inside the platform.
To draft the written rules, use Magic Write — Canva's AI writing tool built into the editor. Click "Magic Write," describe what you need, and it generates the copy inline.

Great Shot, Messy Background

You have a photo of a runner mid-stride on a city street. Dynamic pose, sharp focus, right energy for a sports gear campaign — it's almost perfect. But behind them is a parked delivery truck, three pedestrians, and a construction sign. How do you save the situation without having to reshoot the whole campaign?
Meet Midjourney's Editor
Midjourney's Editor is a full in-browser image editing tool. It handles object cleanup, background removal, and generative fill.
What You'll See Inside the Editor
The Editor has three areas:

• On the left: the tool panel with Smart Select and Paint, which contains the Erase and Restore brushes.
  • In the center: your working canvas.
  • On the right: the results panel where generated outputs appear after each submission.

At the top of the screen is the prompt field — this is where you describe what should fill any area you've erased or selected. Every edit operation follows the same pattern: select or erase an area, write a prompt, and submit.
Meet Stride
For this lesson, you have a new challenge. Stride is a sports gear brand targeting urban sports enthusiasts aged 25-40. They have campaign images that need cleaning up before launch.
Remove the Background With Paint

You have a photo of a cyclist in the city, but there's a truck in the background. The first task: clear the unwanted detail. Paint is the right tool for this: it lets you select messy areas like unwanted objects or background clutter that you want to replace.
Step 1 — Mark What to Erase
Use Paint's Erase brush. Adjust the brush size and erase the truck in the image.

blocks.prompt: Write a prompt in the text field at the top of the Editor to describe what should replace the erased area.
blocks.template: Extend the surrounding [setting] seamlessly into the selected area --no [what to exclude]

blocks.text: Step 3 — Remove the Detail

Once the mask covers the truck cleanly and the prompt is ready, click Submit Edit. Midjourney fills the painted region to match the adjacent pixels and returns 8 output options. Choose the one that blends best with the surrounding scene.
Cleanup prompts work best when they describe what the area should look like — material, color, and lighting condition. Those three inputs give the model something to match.
blocks.title: Prompt Pro Tip

blocks.text: Isolate a Subject With Smart Select

The truck is gone. Now Stride needs another output — a transparent PNG of a runner for a product webpage. Smart Select handles this: it creates a selection mask using positive and negative points — no manual painting required.
Step 1 — Mark What to Keep

Click Smart Select to activate it, then click directly on the runner. These are positive points that tell the tool to include this area in the mask. Add enough points across the full figure to cover the subject completely.
Step 2 — Mark What to Remove
Click on Exclude and click the background. These are negative points that exclude those areas from the mask.
Step 3 — Remove the Background
Click Erase Background. Everything outside the mask is removed. The result is a transparent PNG with the runner isolated.

Smart Select handles edge detection automatically — it reads color and contrast boundaries to separate the subject from the background. For a runner against a street, the contrast between clothing and pavement gives the model clear edges to work with.
Replace the Sky With Generative Fill

The runner is cut out and ready to drop into any layout. One more element is holding the Stride campaign back: on one of the images, the sky is flat and grey. It's not the mood a sports gear campaign needs. This is where generative fill comes in.

The difference between cleanup and generative fill is scale and intent. Cleanup erases a small area and asks the model to continue what's already there. Generative fill erases a large area and introduces something new, while matching the surrounding image's lighting and style.

blocks.text: Export for Use

Once the edit is done, click Download Image at the bottom right of the Editor to save the file at original resolution with transparency preserved. For a higher-quality output — for wide-format banners or print — click Upscale to Gallery first, then download from there.
You've done three targeted edits. Now, the truck is gone, the runner is cut out, and the sky is replaced. What started as "almost usable" is now campaign-ready!

  • Generative fill introduces new content: Match the original image's light direction and temperature in the prompt — a fill that ignores lighting will always feel like a composite.
  • Export to match the use case: Download directly for standard digital use. Upscale to Gallery first for wide-format or print output.

Three Posts by Friday

You've built the foundation of any design work: prompting for better designs, a visual direction, a brand kit, and editing.

Now those skills have a deadline. A client needs three social media posts — Instagram feed, Instagram Story, and Facebook banner — by Friday. This lesson walks through the full production process!
Meet Bloom

Bloom is a plant care app that reminds users when to water, fertilize, and repot their houseplants. It's launching next week, and it needs a set of social media creatives that feel as alive as the product itself.
The brand direction is soft and natural — warm greens, terracotta, clean, rounded type, lifestyle imagery of plants in real homes. The brief: create a launch post set that works across formats.
Start With One Strong Visual

Every format adaptation starts from a single source image. Get that right first. A strong hero image — well-composed, on-brand, with a clear focal point — adapts to any ratio without losing its impact.

Let's create the visual in Midjourney to get a realistic, high-quality result.

blocks.prompt: Prompt Midjourney for Bloom's hero image. Use "--no" to exclude anything clinical or artificial.
blocks.template: Create [output] for Bloom, a plant care app. Style: [style direction]. Mood: [mood]. Colors: warm greens, terracotta, soft natural light --no [what to exclude].

blocks.text: These images work as a starting point because they have a clear subject, consistent lighting, and enough negative space to layer text onto. Those three qualities are what make an image adaptable.
Format Is Not Just Size

Adapting a design to a new format isn't just resizing, but rethinking the hierarchy. An Instagram rectangle puts the subject at the center. A Story puts it top-and-center with space below for a CTA. A Facebook banner puts it left with text on the right.
Resize With Canva
Let's say you've built an Instagram post draft. Use Canva's "Resize" feature to change the format of the visual.
Instagram Formats
Resize handles the mechanical part. Your job is to check what the resize did to the composition: whether the focal point is still visible, the text has breathing room, and the CTA is readable.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! Repositioning the background preserves the brand consistency of the set. Regenerating from scratch breaks the visual thread across formats.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Regenerating produces a different image — and a different image means a different set. Adaptation keeps the visual thread intact. Fix the crop, don't replace the source.

options.label: Regenerate the image in Midjourney at a 9:16 ratio and restart the adaptation from scratch
Reposition the image to restore the focal point within the new frame
Use a different image for the Story format — some images only work at specific ratios

blocks.question: You've resized the Bloom hero image from an Instagram rectangular post (4:5) to Instagram Story (9:16). The plant is now partially cropped. What's the right fix?

blocks.text: The Facebook Banner

The Instagram formats share a vertical logic — subject prominent, CTA below. The Facebook banner is horizontal, which flips the hierarchy entirely. The subject on one side, the text anchored to another, and the image supports the message.
Use Resize to generate the banner dimensions, then reposition the plant image to either side of the frame. Another half needs clear space — that's where the headline and tagline will sit.

Every format has its own hierarchy: what the viewer sees first, where their eye goes next, and where the CTA lands. Adapting well means checking all three after every resize.
  • Instagram feed: Subject centered, copy layered over negative space
  • Instagram Story: Subject top-and-center, CTA in the lower third
  • Facebook banner: Subject left, headline and CTA right

For Bloom's launch, they want a targeted Instagram ad. The image needs to show what Bloom looks like. The copy should say what it does and what to do next. Headline, one supporting line, CTA — three elements are enough to communicate the idea.

Before You Publish — One Check
The Bloom visuals were generated in Midjourney. Before they go live on a brand account, one question needs an answer: what does Midjourney's license allow for commercial use?

The answer lives on Midjourney's Terms of Service page — linked in the footer of docs.midjourney.com. Look for "Content Rights" and confirm it applies to your plan. Paid plans include commercial rights. Free plans do not.

From Prompt to Polished App Screen

AI can generate a mobile app home screen from a single prompt — a structured first draft with navigation, content sections, and action buttons.

This lesson covers the full process: generating a UI layout in Uizard, evaluating it against core UX principles, and refining it into something a real user could navigate without confusion.
What You're Building

UI (user interface) is what the user sees: the buttons, layout, colors, and text on screen. UX (user experience) is how the user moves through it: whether the screen is clear, logical, and easy to act on. AI tools can produce UI. Making it a good UX is the designer's job.

In this lesson, you'll build an app called Loop — a habit tracker for adults building daily routines. The home screen needs to show today's habits, a streak counter, a progress summary, and a clear way to check in.

The tool for the first draft is Uizard — an AI-powered UI generator that produces editable layouts from text prompts. Open Uizard, start a new project, select Mobile as the project type, describe the app in the text field, then choose Generate with Autodesigner to reach the prompt field.

Note: Uizard's Autodesigner prompt field has a 150-symbol limit. Keep the prompt short and specific: describe the core use case, the key sections, and the visual tone. Everything else Uizard fills in based on the project type.

blocks.text: Explore What Uizard Generated
Click any page to see the interaction flow — arrows connecting screens, each one configurable.
Click an arrow to set interactions:

• Type defines what happens when the user taps the element: "Go to screen" or "Open link."
  • Destination is where the interaction leads: Home, Signup, Welcome, Add Item, Statistics, or any other screen in the project.
  • Animation is how the transition between screens looks: Fade, Slide Left, Slide Right, Slide Up, Slide Down.
This is how Uizard maps the user journey: screen appearance and the transitions between them.
Now you have your first draft. Aside from what you requested, Uizard generated a welcome and a signup page with content sections, buttons, and placeholder text.
If you want to change any of that, the left navigation panel gives you everything Uizard offers.

Uizard reliably handles structure: navigation placement, section grouping, and component sizing relative to each other. The layout is logical — a real user could navigate it. But structure isn't design. Before moving forward, it's worth looking at what the generation got right and what it didn't.
Uizard's Magic
To evaluate what Uizard generated, use its Magic feature, the AI layer built into the editor. It can generate additional screens, swap images, apply new themes, rewrite content, and more.

feedbackIncorrect.text: ChatGPT can reason about design principles, but works better when it has specific data to react to — like a heatmap. Human critique is valuable too, but slower and more subjective for a first-pass evaluation. Uizard's Design Review works directly on the live design and gives you precise visual data on where attention lands. Start there, then layer in other perspectives.

blocks.text: Run a Design Review With Magic
The most useful Magic function for evaluating a generated design is Design Review. Activate it from the Magic menu. Click on the screen you want to review, then hit the Magic button above it.
Design Review flags hierarchy problems visually. It produces a heatmap showing visual attention density (where users' eyes are likely to go).

• Red/yellow = high attention
  • Blue/green = low
This is Uizard's heatmap for the Loop's "Add item" screen. What Magic doesn't fix: hierarchy decisions and copy. Design Review will show you the problem. Deciding what to do about it is up to you.

blocks.exampleResponse: What's wrong (based on the heatmap): — No clear flow → attention jumps between title, days, time cards, and slider — CTA is weak → "Add" doesn't dominate — Inconsistent components → pills, cards, slider, toggle = cognitive load How to improve: — Create a clear order: Name → Days → Time → Duration → CTA — Unify components: use similar patterns (e.g., pills for all selections) — Replace slider: use presets (5 / 10 / 15 / 30 min) — Fix CTA: make it the most prominent element (full-width, high contrast) — Simplify toggle: use a single switch instead of Yes/No
blocks.prompt: Upload the Design Review heatmap to ChatGPT and ask it to identify UX problems and suggest fixes.
blocks.template: You are a senior UX designer. Analyze this [visual output] for a mobile habit tracker [screen name]. Identify key UX problems: [evaluation criteria]. Prioritize issues by impact on completion.

blocks.text:
ChatGPT identified three problems: a weak CTA, inconsistent components, and no clear order for the user to follow. 

The first fix recommended: establish a logical sequence. Name → Days → Time → Duration → CTA. That means the copy needs to change first — once the labels are clear, the structural fixes follow.

blocks.exampleResponse: 1. Name Label: Habit name: e.g., Drink water 2. Days Section title: Schedule 3. Time Section title: Time of day 4. Duration Section title: Duration Options (recommended instead of slider): 5 min | 10 min | 15 min | 30 min 5. Optional setting Label: Show on home screen (use toggle, default ON — no extra copy needed) 6. CTA Primary button: Create habit
blocks.prompt: Ask ChatGPT to write UI copy for the "Add habit" screen following the recommended order.
blocks.template: You are [role]. Write UI copy for [screen name] screen of a habit tracker app called Loop. Follow this order: Name → Days → Time → Duration → CTA. Tone: [tone direction].

blocks.text: "Create habit" names the action and frames it as meaningful. "Add" did neither. "Schedule" and "Time of day" tell the user what each section is for. The copy gave the screen a logical reading order.
Evaluate Against Three UX Principles
The next step is evaluating what still needs to change structurally. Three principles cover the most common problems in AI-generated mobile screens — and in most UI design in general.

Hierarchy = what does the user see first? On a well-designed screen, the most important element has the most visual weight: larger, bolder, higher contrast, or positioned at the top of the natural reading path.
Clarity = does every element communicate its purpose without explanation? Labels, buttons, and icons should be self-evident. If a user has to guess what a button does, clarity has failed.
Flow = what does the user do next? Every screen should have one primary action that's more prominent than everything else. If all actions look equal, the user hesitates.

feedbackCorrect.text: Nailed it! Hierarchy is about visual priority — which element has the most weight. When everything looks the same, the screen has no hierarchy. The user's eye has nowhere to go.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Flow is about the primary action path — and equal visual weight does affect it. But flow breaks down as a consequence of missing hierarchy, not as the root cause. A screen with no visual priority has no hierarchy first, and no clear flow second. Fix hierarchy, and flow often follows.

options.label: Hierarchy — nothing tells the user where to look first or what matters most
Flow — the equal sizing means the user has no obvious primary action to take
Clarity — the equal sizing makes it hard to understand what each element does

blocks.question: On the generated Loop home screen, the streak counter, the habit list, and the check-in button all have the same font size and visual weight. Which UX principle does this violate most directly?

blocks.text: The fixes are targeted; it's not a redesign. Change the CTA and rewrite labels with real copy that reflects what Loop does. Swap the duration slider for preset options (5, 10, 15, 30 min) to reduce cognitive load. Simplify the toggle to a single switch with a clear label.
With these changes applied, the screen looks like this!
Fix the Principle, Not Just the Element

When you resize the check-in button, you're fixing hierarchy. When you rewrite "Habit 1" to "Morning walk — tap to complete", you're fixing clarity. When you move the streak counter to the top, you're fixing flow. Name the principle before you make the change — it keeps fixes purposeful, not cosmetic.

• AI generates structure, you generate usability: A generated layout gives you sections, navigation, and component placement. Hierarchy, clarity, and flow come from your decisions — and Uizard's Magic Design Review shows you where the problems are.
  • Heatmaps show what words can't: Design Review's visual attention map tells you which elements are competing for focus and which are disappearing. Use it as your first diagnostic before making any changes.
  • Copy is part of the design: Placeholder labels and generic button text reach real users if left unchanged. Use ChatGPT to write copy that gives every field, button, and section a clear purpose.
  • Fix the principle, not just the element: Unifying components fixes cognitive load. Enlarging the CTA fixes the hierarchy. Rewriting labels fixes clarity. Name the principle before making the change — it keeps fixes purposeful, not cosmetic.

Check What Works

The Bloom social post from previous lessons looks on-brand. The FocusShift landing page copy feels right. But "looks right" and "feels right" aren't the same as "works."

In the last lesson, you gave ChatGPT a heatmap and got back a prioritized list of UX problems for the Loop screen. That same critique approach works on everything else you've built across the guide. Let's dive in!
What's a Useful Critique?

ChatGPT's Loop evaluation worked because the input was specific. That's the same principle you applied to prompts in Lesson 2. Whether you're generating a visual or requesting a critique, the more precisely you define the design, its goal, and what you want evaluated, the more useful the output.

feedbackCorrect.text: This prompt defines role, product, audience, and exact criteria — and asks for prioritization. That last instruction is what separates a ranked action list from an unordered list, where a minor copy issue and a broken CTA carry equal weight.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A prompt that states the role and the audience doesn't mention any specific criteria or prioritization request. Without them, ChatGPT evaluates whatever it notices — and the feedback won't be grounded in what the post is actually trying to do.

options.label: "You are a senior brand designer. Critique this Instagram post for Bloom, a plant care app targeting urban adults aged 25-45. Evaluate: headline clarity, CTA visibility, and whether copy and image are doing different jobs. Flag the highest-impact problem first."

blocks.text: A vague prompt — "what do you think of this design?" — produces a vague response: generic praise, surface observations, no prioritized fixes. A specific prompt defines the design type, the audience, the goal, and the exact dimension you want evaluated.

A useful critique prompt has four parts:
  • Role = "you are a senior brand designer"
  • Context = product, audience, goal
  • Criteria = what specifically to evaluate
  • Priority = "flag the highest-impact problem first"
Miss any one of them and the feedback loses precision.

Before applying any fix, ask, is this a real problem, or a misread of intent? The decision should always be yours.

The FocusShift landing page copy from Lesson 2 has a headline, a tagline, and a CTA. It was written to feel warm and encouraging — but warm copy and persuasive copy aren't automatically the same thing. The critique prompt checks whether it does the job it was built to do.

Let's remember what the copy sounded like: Headline: "Your best work happens in 25 minutes" Tagline: "A simple way to manage deep work with steady, timed sessions, so you can stay present, make progress, and finish what matters." CTA: "Start a focused session"

The landing page goal is to convert visitors into app downloads — adults aged 40-60 who want to build focus habits. The criteria: whether the headline communicates a clear benefit, whether the tagline supports or repeats it, and whether the CTA creates enough momentum to act.

blocks.text: Start With Tasks, Not Tools
Tools are only useful relative to what you're trying to do. The right starting point when building an AI design workflow is your actual recurring tasks.

A recurring task is something you do regularly enough that a faster, more reliable process would compound over time. Generating a hero image for a new campaign. Resizing assets for multiple platforms. Writing copy for a landing page update. Those are tasks worth building a workflow around.

A workflow only reduces friction if it's built around what you actually do — not what you plan to do, what looks impressive, or what the guide covered. 

Recurring tasks come first. Tools follow.
blocks.title: 💡 A Workflow Serves Your Tasks

blocks.text: Build Your Workflow Map
A workflow map is a simple document: your most common design tasks in one column, the tool that handles each one in the second, and a one-line note on when that tool is the right choice in the third.
You don't need to map every task you've ever done. Four to six recurring tasks are enough to build a workflow worth using. More than that, and the map becomes a reference document you never open.

blocks.text: The New Tool Problem

New AI design tools appear constantly. Some are meaningfully better than what you're using. Most are variations on what already exists. The challenge is deciding which new tools actually earn a place in a workflow that already works.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on! Quality is one factor, not the only one. Transition cost — learning the interface, updating prompt templates, checking licensing — is real. A better tool earns its place when the quality gain outweighs the cost of switching, and when it fits the tasks you actually do.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A quality improvement is worth pursuing — but "better quality" doesn't automatically mean "worth switching." A tool that's 10% better but requires rebuilding your prompt library and checking new licensing terms may not be worth disrupting a workflow that already produces good results.

Test Before You Commit

Before treating the workflow map as final, run it once on a real brief — even a small one. A campaign image, a landing page headline, a single resized asset. The first real use reveals friction points the map didn't predict: a tool that takes longer than expected, a step that's missing, a handoff between tools that breaks the flow. One test run is worth more than a perfectly written map that's never been used.
